## Proverbs 17 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1: "Better a dry morsel in quietness than a house full of feasting with strife."

The traditional reading emphasizes domestic peace over material abundance. A "dry morsel" was bread without dipping sauce—a meager, unappealing meal. Yet the blessing of peace and quietness is so great that it outweighs a house "full of sacrifices" (the KJV reading, referring to fellowship offerings whose meat was eaten in feasts). These sacrificial feasts, though sumptuous, often degenerated into excess and quarreling (1 Sam 1:5–6, 13; 2:13). Gill notes that the Hebrew word for "dry morsel" carries a sense of something broken, old, or stale—yet with peace in the family and peace with God, it surpasses rich fare with strife. The Pulpit Commentary compares the early church's love-feasts (agapae) that were desecrated by selfishness (1 Cor 11:20ff).

### v. 2: "A wise servant will rule over a disgraceful son and share his inheritance as one of the brothers."

Character trumps birthright. Ellicott notes this was "strikingly exhibited in the case of Ziba," who gained Mephibosheth's property (2 Sam 16:4). Eliezer would have been Abraham's heir had Isaac not been born (Gen 15:3). Guzik quotes Waltke: "Contrary to judicial law and custom, one's virtue, not the privilege of birth, ultimately counts for more." Gill sees a typological application: Gentiles (as a "wise servant") become fellow-heirs with the children of Israel. The Pulpit Commentary adds that slaves could be raised to executor status, dividing the inheritance among the heirs.

### v. 3: "A crucible for silver and a furnace for gold, but the LORD is the tester of hearts."

Silver and gold are refined by fire in crucibles and furnaces; only God can test and purify the human heart. G. Campbell Morgan (quoted by Guzik) notes two thoughts: first, the heart will yield to no force other than God's; second, God does indeed try the heart. Ellicott adds that God tests hearts "by allowing sorrows and temptations to assail them, in order that they may come out of the trial as pure gold" (cf. 1 Pet 1:7; Mal 3:3). Trapp (quoted by Guzik): "He therefore tries us, that he may make us know what is in us, what dross, what pure metal."

### v. 4: "A wicked man listens to evil lips; a liar gives ear to a destructive tongue."

Evil people not only speak lies—they eagerly receive them. Trapp: "It is an ill sign of a vicious nature to be apt to believe scandalous reports of godly men." Kidner (quoted by Guzik): "Evil words die without a welcome; and the welcome gives us away." The Pulpit Commentary: "Like mates with like"—a bad man delights in those who counsel wickedness, and a liar listens avidly to any tale that injures a neighbour. This proverb diagnoses a corrupt heart by what it loves to hear.

### v. 5: "He who mocks the poor insults their Maker; whoever gloats over calamity will not go unpunished."

Mocking the poor is an insult to God because He made both the poor person and the mocker (cf. Prov 14:31). Morgan (quoted by Guzik) clarifies: "The first part of this proverb does not teach, as is so often stated, that poverty is from God. Rather, it recognizes the inherent rights of every man in God, notwithstanding his poverty." The second line condemns *epichairekakia* (a Greek term Aristotle used for rejoicing at others' misfortunes). Job counted himself free from this sin (Job 31:29). Gill notes that the Targum renders "reproaches his Maker" as "provokes his Creator to anger."

### v. 6: "Grandchildren are the crown of the aged, and the glory of a son is his father."

Waltke (quoted by Guzik): "The proverb pictures them gathered around the aged parent like a crowning diadem." Garrett (quoted by Guzik) notes the "profound assertion of the psychological interdependence of the generations." The Pulpit Commentary adds that in the East, numerous offspring were considered a great blessing—a guarantee of family stability. Fathers should live so that children glory in them; conversely, children can bring shame (Kidner references Isa 3:5; Mic 7:6; 2 Tim 3:2–4).

### v. 7: "Eloquent words are unfit for a fool; how much worse are lying lips to a ruler!"

Excellent (or "arrogant, pretentious") speech does not suit a *nabal* (a vile or base fool—see Isa 32:6). It is incongruous. But far worse is lying in the mouth of a *nadib* (a noble, liberal, princely person). The principle is *noblesse oblige*. Ellicott renders: "Superfluous or pretentious words become not a vile person; much less do lying lips a prince." Trapp: "God likes not fair words from a foul mouth." Gill applies it to the Gospel: excellent speech (sound doctrine) is unfit in the mouth of a wicked man.

### v. 8: "A bribe is a charm to its giver; wherever he turns, he succeeds."

There is a satirical tone here. The Hebrew *'eben chen* ("a stone of grace") suggests a bribe functions like a magic charm or dazzling jewel in the eyes of its possessor. Guzik notes: "The proverb is expressing this reality from the viewpoint of the one giving the bribe—it works." The Pulpit Commentary says the bribe inflames the recipient with sordid hopes so that "wheresoever he turneth himself he dealeth wisely"—he exerts all his skill to earn his wages. The verse states a common reality without endorsing it.

### v. 9: "Whoever conceals an offense promotes love, but he who brings it up separates friends."

To "cover" a transgression means to forgive, overlook, and not constantly revisit a wrong done against you—this "seeks love" (1 Cor 14:1; cf. Prov 10:12). The one who "repeats a matter" harps on old grievances and alienates even the closest friend (*'alluph*, a chief friend). Kidner notes the verb may indicate tale-bearing or "harping on a matter." The Pulpit Commentary quotes Ecclus. 19:7ff: "If thou hast heard a word, let it die with thee."

### v. 10: "A rebuke cuts into a man of discernment deeper than a hundred lashes cut into a fool."

One well-aimed verbal rebuke penetrates deeper into a wise person than a hundred blows into a fool. The problem is not the correction but the recipient. Morgan: "The finer the disposition, the less is needed to correct it." The Septuagint (quoted in Pulpit) sharpens the contrast: "A threat breaks the heart of a prudent man; a fool even scourged feels it not." Gill: "Stripes only reach the back, but not the heart of a fool."

### v. 11: "An evil man seeks only rebellion; a cruel messenger will be sent against him."

The Hebrew can be read either as "an evil man seeks only rebellion" or (as Ellicott, Pulpit prefer) "a rebellious man seeks only evil." From an ancient Near Eastern perspective, rebellion against the king invites swift, pitiless retribution—the "cruel messenger" (the royal executioner; cf. 1 Kgs 2:29, 34, 46). The Septuagint reads "the Lord shall send a pitiless angel against him," giving it a theological dimension of divine judgment. Guzik notes the "cruel messenger" could also refer to storms, pestilence, or any misfortune sent as God's retribution.

### v. 12: "It is better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool in his folly."

The Syrian bear robbed of her young was proverbially ferocious (2 Sam 17:8; Hos 13:8). Yet even that is safer than encountering a fool in the full heat of his folly—whether rage, lust, or stubborn rebellion. Guzik: "The human, who is supposed to be intelligent and rational, in such folly becomes more dangerous than the beast." Gill applies it to false teachers: "such are the followers of the man of sin, who have no mercy on the souls of men they deceive."

### v. 13: "If anyone returns evil for good, evil will never leave his house."

This upsets God's moral order. Trapp (quoted by Guzik): "To render good for evil is divine, good for good is human, evil for evil is brutish, evil for good is devilish." Kidner notes this proverb was "very near the bone" for Solomon: both his parents (David and Bathsheba) had so repaid the devoted Uriah and received the sentence of line 2 (2 Sam 12:10ff). Clarke: "As many persons are guilty of the sin of ingratitude… it is no wonder we find so much wretchedness among men."

### v. 14: "To start a quarrel is to release a flood; so abandon the dispute before it breaks out."

The image is of a small leak in a dam that, once started, quickly becomes an uncontrollable torrent. Waltke (quoted by Guzik): "The seepage starts from a small aperture, but under built-up pressure it quickly bursts open." Kidner: "Opening such a sluice lets loose more than one can predict, control or retrieve." Therefore wisdom stops contention before it starts. Trapp compares it to the Dutch maintaining their dikes: they keep them with little cost because they look narrowly to them and make them up in time. The Pulpit Commentary notes Solomon's own pools and reservoirs near Bethlehem made the image vivid.

### v. 15: "Acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous—both are detestable to the LORD."

Both perversions of justice are equally abominable to God. The Pulpit Commentary notes this was "a fruitful source of evil in Israel, and a constant topic of reproach in the mouth of the prophets" (Isa 5:23; 1 Sam 8:3; Ps 82:2). Waltke (quoted by Guzik) makes a striking point: "The proverb corrects the popular misconception that it is better to set free ten guilty persons than to condemn one innocent person. Both are an abomination to the Lord."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/17.htm

### v. 16: "Why should the fool have money in his hand with no intention of buying wisdom?"

Wisdom has a price—the fear of the LORD, humility, willingness to receive correction—but the fool has "no heart for it." The Pulpit Commentary explains: the fool thinks wisdom can be purchased with money (as one might pay a teacher), but lacks the mental and spiritual capacity to receive it. The Vulgate reads: *Quid prodest stulto habere divitias, cum sapientiam emere non possit?* ("What does it profit a fool to have riches, since he cannot buy wisdom?"). Guzik: "The nature of the fool requires that they have no heart to pay the price of wisdom."

### v. 17: "A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity."

The traditional reading (shared across all traditions) is that a true friend loves consistently—in fair weather and foul—and a true brother reveals himself especially in times of trouble. Ellicott renders: "The (true) friend loveth at all times, and (as) a brother is born for adversity." The Pulpit Commentary cites Cicero: *Amicus certus in re incerta cernitur* ("A sure friend is known in uncertain times").

**Spurgeon (Baptist):** In his sermon "The Unrivalled Friend," Spurgeon lifts this text to Christ: "There is a Friend, blessed for ever be his name, who loveth at all times; there is a Brother who in an emphatic sense was born for adversity. That friend is Jesus." He notes that Christ was born first to deliver us from the great adversity of the fall, and has the peculiar art of sympathizing with all in adversity—"Every pang that ever rends a human heart has first tried its keen edge on him."

**Desiring God (Reformed Baptist — John Piper):** The article "The Best Friends Are Born for Adversity" applies this proverb to the church: "Our churches should be places where friends move toward pain, suffering, and hardship in love, not away from it in selfish fear." Jesus is the perfect friend who "loves at all times, no matter what they did to him, to his very last breath."

**Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic):** Notes that Bridges applied the proverb to Christ: "The ancient Jews applied this proverb to Christ, adducing it as a testimony that the divine Messiah would by his incarnation become the Brother of man."

### v. 18: "A man lacking judgment strikes hands in pledge and puts up security for his neighbor."

The traditional warning against suretyship (cf. Prov 6:1ff; 11:15; 20:16). To "strike hands" was to seal a pledge. The Pulpit Commentary calls it the "weakness which, for the sake of perhaps worthless companions, lets itself be hampered and endangered by others' obligations." Gill: "he that is surety for another is never sure himself."

### v. 19: "He who loves transgression loves strife; he who builds his gate high invites destruction."

Loving sin and loving conflict go together. The one who "builds his gate high" (constructs an ostentatious, lofty entrance to his house) is exalting himself above his neighbour and assuming a lifestyle beyond his rank (Bridges, quoted by Guzik). Clarke alternatively suggests "gate" may be a metaphor for the mouth—proud, arrogant boasting that kindles strife. The Pulpit Commentary (cut off) appears to concur with the ostentation interpretation. Either way, pride invites destruction.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-17/
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/17.htm

### v. 20: "The one with a perverse heart finds no good, and he whose tongue is deceitful falls into trouble."

The perverse (or "froward," KJV) heart and the deceitful tongue go together. Such a person "finds no good" because he is an abomination to God (Prov 11:20) and gains no blessing from Him (Ellicott). Guzik adds: "The one filled with deceit will only find corruption and deceit in others."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-17/
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/17.htm

### v. 21: "A man fathers a fool to his own grief; the father of a fool has no joy."

Two Hebrew words for "fool" appear: *kesil* (the obstinate, self-confident fool) in the first line and *nabal* (the base, morally vile fool) in the second (Ellicott). To be parent to either brings sorrow, not joy. Trapp (quoted by Guzik) recalls William the Conqueror and Henry II, both of whom died in grief over rebellious children.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-17/
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/17.htm

### v. 22: "A joyful heart is good medicine, but a broken spirit dries up the bones."

Ellicott renders: "A merry heart makes good a recovery" (i.e., promotes healing). Guzik: "It has been said—no doubt based on this proverb—that laughter is the best medicine." Conversely, a broken (crushed) spirit has physiological effects: "dry bones" signify unhealthiness and lifelessness (cf. Ezek 37:1–14). Ross (quoted by Guzik): "Fat bones means a healthy body (Prov 3:8; 15:30; 16:24), but dry bones signify unhealthiness." The Pulpit Commentary connects religious gladness with this proverb (cf. Phil 3:1; 4:4).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-17/
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/17.htm

### v. 23: "A wicked man takes a covert bribe to subvert the course of justice."

Ellicott notes the bribe is taken "from the bosom"—the folds of the garment in which the bribe was concealed, ready to be slipped into the judge's hand. This is the "covert" (secret) bribe. The perversion of justice through bribery is a recurring theme in Proverbs (cf. vv. 8, 15, 26; also 14:5, 25; 18:5; 19:5, 9, 28).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-17/
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/17.htm

### v. 24: "Wisdom is the focus of the discerning, but the eyes of a fool wander to the ends of the earth."

The wise person perceives wisdom right before him—it is present, accessible, the focus of his attention. The fool's eyes roam to "the ends of the earth," chasing fantasies, novelties, and distant speculations while missing the instruction right in front of him. Ellicott: "He is looking for her everywhere, while all the time she lies straight before him" (cf. Deut 30:11–14). Guzik: "The wise person keeps their eyes on what is near and necessary."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-17/
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/17.htm

### v. 25: "A foolish son brings grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him."

This verse returns to the theme of v. 21, now explicitly including the mother. The foolish son brings grief to the father and bitterness specifically to the mother who bore him—suggesting a particularly deep pain for the one who carried and nurtured him.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-17/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/proverbs-17.html

### v. 26: "It is surely not good to punish the innocent or to flog a noble for his honesty."

This returns to the justice theme (vv. 15, 23). Ellicott notes "punish" here especially means fining, and "to strike" means to scourge—the penalty for those convicted in court (Deut 25:1–3). To flog a noble (*nadib*) "for his honesty" (or uprightness) is a perversion of justice. The Bridgeway Commentary connects this to widespread court corruption in the writer's day.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-17/
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/17.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/proverbs-17.html

### v. 27: "A man of knowledge restrains his words, and a man of understanding maintains a calm spirit."

Ellicott renders: "He that restrains his words hath knowledge, and one who is cool of temper is a man of understanding." The verse counsels both verbal restraint and emotional composure. The "calm spirit" (or "excellent/cool spirit") is a mark of true understanding.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-17/
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/17.htm

### v. 28: "Even a fool is considered wise if he keeps silent, and discerning when he holds his tongue."

The classic "dry" proverb: silence can disguise folly. Guzik calls it "a dry but practical bit of encouragement." If even a fool gains a reputation for wisdom simply by keeping his mouth shut, how much more should the wise practice restraint. This verse fittingly caps the chapter's themes of speech, wisdom, and folly.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-17/

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

Most of Proverbs 17 consists of general wisdom sayings on which the major Protestant traditions substantially agree. The areas where distinct emphases appear:

**Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill):** Spurgeon reads v. 17 Christologically—Jesus is the ultimate "friend who loves at all times" and the "brother born for adversity." This is a hallmark of Spurgeon's preaching: lifting wisdom texts to Christ. Gill, writing earlier (1746), provides extensive Hebrew word analysis and occasionally draws typological applications (e.g., v. 2 as the Gentiles sharing Israel's inheritance).

**Reformed Baptist / New Calvinism (Desiring God — John Piper):** Emphasizes v. 17 as a call to cruciform friendship in the local church. The article "The Best Friends Are Born for Adversity" stresses that "Jesus didn't condone their sin, but he didn't run from them because of it"—a nuance relevant to debates about church discipline and grace.

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word — David Guzik):** Guzik's commentary is broadly evangelical but published through a charismatic ministry. His notes on v. 3 quote G. Campbell Morgan, emphasizing that "the heart will yield to no force other than that of God." His treatment of v. 22 ("a joyful heart is good medicine") resonates with charismatic emphasis on joy, healing, and the connection between spiritual and physical well-being.

**Anglican (Ellicott):** Ellicott's commentary (19th c.) provides concise philological notes. He emphasizes the translation nuance of v. 7 (the "fool" as *nabal*, the "prince" as *nadib*—a liberal/noble person) and v. 17 (reading "and as a brother is born for adversity"). His notes tend toward precise lexical clarification.
